ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Host immune defense comprises innate and adaptive mechanisms that protect the body from infection and injury. Clinicians must recognise how these systems fail, interpret relevant tests, and intervene appropriately.

sections.p: The immune system uses physical barriers, cellular defenses, and soluble factors to detect and eliminate pathogens. Understanding the sequence of events helps pinpoint where failure leads to disease.
b: Innate immunity acts within minutes; adaptive immunity develops over days
Key cells: neutrophils, macrophages, dendritic cells, T‑cells, B‑cells

sections.p: Identify the immune defect or excessive response by correlating history, physical findings, and targeted investigations.

t.a: Skin test or interferon‑γ release assay for TB
t.b: Does latent TB trigger an immune response?

sections.p: Address the underlying cause, then support the immune system and prevent complications.
b: Treat infections with appropriate antimicrobials; avoid unnecessary antibiotics that disrupt microbiota
Use immunoglobulin replacement for proven antibody deficiency
Start antiretroviral therapy promptly in HIV to restore CD4 counts
Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms in asplenic or complement‑deficient patients
Consider prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., TMP‑SMX) for severe neutropenia

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical practice.
b: Adaptive immunity: T‑cell mediated (cellular) vs B‑cell mediated (humoral)
Low CD4 count = opportunistic infections; high neutrophil count = bacterial infection
Biofilms shield bacteria from both antibiotics and immune cells

whenToSeekHelp: Severe sepsis or septic shock, unexplained fever with neutropenia, rapidly progressive skin infection, new neurological deficits in immunocompromised patients

faq.q: Why do some patients with normal white counts still get infections?
faq.a: Functional defects (e.g., NADPH oxidase deficiency) can impair killing despite normal numbers.

faq.q: How does a biofilm affect immune defense?
faq.a: It creates a physical barrier that prevents immune cells and antibodies from reaching bacteria, leading to chronic infection.

faq.q: When is it appropriate to give prophylactic antibiotics?
faq.a: In patients with prolonged neutropenia (<500 cells/µL) or severe T‑cell deficiency to prevent opportunistic infections.

exam: Explain the steps of the innate immune response to a bacterial skin infection and where it can fail.
Interpret a CBC with neutropenia and low IgG in a child with recurrent pneumonia; propose next investigations and management.
Describe how HIV infection alters CD4 counts and the clinical implications for opportunistic infections.
